newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shouldn't use dollar as trade tool -- Rubin.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shouldn't use dollar as trade tool -- Rubin.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Tuesday brushed aside U.S. automakers' complaints about the strength of the dollar, saying that the key to competitiveness is efficiency.
"I do not believe we should use our dollar as an instrument of trade policy," he told reporters following a speech to the American Association of Retired Persons.
He said that U.S. industry is more competitive than it has been for a long time across a broad array of industries.

In his speech to the AARP, Rubin reiterated the Clinton administration's opposition to a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution, saying it would be a "terrible, terrible mistake" if it were adopted.
"It is an uphill battle to defeat it but it is doable," Rubin said. He said that President Clinton is "troubled" by the amendment and is "very deeply engaged" in the fight to defeat it.
Passage of such an amendment could sap some of the political will needed to make the tough decisions necessary to actually balance the budget, Rubin added.
It would also pose an additional risk to social security, Rubin said.

He sounded a cautious note about proposals to privatize social security by allowing some of the trust fund's money to be invested in the stockmarket, although he stopped well short of rejecting such suggestions outright.
While it is "very tempting" to go that route given that stock prices have risen eightfold since 1982, he said, "it's kind of a heady atmosphere in which to be thinking of that."
"There are a lot of issues around risk and volatility ... that would have to be looked at with great care before we did that," Rubin said.

Rubin said that Clinton was committed to fully protecting social security against the ravages of inflation. But he also noted that the vast majority of experts agree that the Consumer Price Index, which is used to set cost-of-living increases for social security benefits, overstates inflation.
"You should try to adjust that if you can find a way to do it," he said. He said that politicians should wait to see if expert opinion can coalesce around a certain position before acting, however.

Rubin was also cautious about calls for wholesale reform of the U.S. tax system. While many reform proposals sound attractive initially they have enormous ramifications that need to be considered, he said.
